title: Data Wrangling with dplyr and tidyr
text: Wrangling is the controlled movement from a source table to an analysis-ready table. A good pipeline makes its assumptions visible: which rows are included, which fields are derived, what the row grain is, and how multiple tables are related. The tidyverse expresses these decisions as a readable sequence.

title: Data Wrangling with dplyr and tidyr
text:
The core verbs

filter(): choose rows
filter() keeps observations whose conditions are TRUE.
mtcars |>
  filter(cyl == 6, mpg > 20)
Use & for “and,” | for “or,” and %in% for membership in a set. A condition involving NA does not keep the row, so decide whether missing values should be excluded or reported separately.


select(): choose columns
select() defines the analysis view without changing the underlying data.
mtcars |>
  select(mpg, cyl, hp, wt)
Use starts_with(), contains(), and where() for systematic selection. Avoid selecting columns by position in production code; names communicate intent and survive schema changes better.


mutate(): create or modify columns
mutate() preserves the row count and adds derived fields.
mtcars |>
  mutate(
    power_to_weight = hp / wt,
    efficiency_band = if_else(mpg >= 20, "Higher", "Lower")
  )
Check units and denominators. A ratio is not automatically an average, and a per-unit measure can be misleading when the denominator is small.


summarize(): collapse rows
summary() computes one or more values from the current group. Without group_by(), it returns one row for the entire table.
mtcars |>
  summarize(
    vehicles = n(),
    average_mpg = mean(mpg),
    median_hp = median(hp)
  )
If missing values are possible, make the rule explicit and report the usable count. n() counts rows; n_distinct(customer_id) counts unique entities.


group_by(): set the level of analysis
group_by() changes the context in which summarize() and some mutate() operations evaluate.
mtcars |>
  group_by(cyl) |>
  summarize(
    vehicles = n(),
    average_mpg = mean(mpg),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  arrange(desc(average_mpg))
The .groups = "drop" choice prevents an invisible grouping state from leaking into later calculations. Treat grouping as part of the metric definition: “average MPG by cylinder count” is different from “average MPG across all vehicles.”


arrange(): order rows
arrange() sorts a table for inspection or presentation.
mtcars |>
  arrange(desc(mpg), wt)
Sorting does not change the values or ranking definition. If ties matter, add a stable secondary key.

title: Data Wrangling with dplyr and tidyr
section: Joins: combine tables without losing control
text:
Joins: combine tables without losing control
Joins match rows through keys. Before joining, document whether the key is unique in each table.
library(tibble)

vehicles <- rownames_to_column(mtcars, var = "model") |>
  as_tibble()

classification <- tibble(
  model = c("Mazda RX4", "Duster 360", "Honda Civic"),
  market = c("Sport", "Performance", "Compact")
)

vehicles |>
  left_join(classification, by = "model")
left_join(x, y) preserves every row of x and appends matching fields from y. Use it when x is the analysis population and y is a lookup table. inner_join() keeps only matched rows and is appropriate when unmatched records should not enter the analysis, but it can silently shrink the population.
Always audit joins:
vehicles |> count(model) |> filter(n > 1)
classification |> count(model) |> filter(n > 1)

before <- nrow(vehicles)
after <- vehicles |> left_join(classification, by = "model") |> nrow()
c(before = before, after = after)
Unexpected row multiplication usually means the supposed key is not unique. An AI assistant will often write a join that runs while ignoring this grain problem.
crumbs: Data Wrangling with dplyr and tidyr

title: Data Wrangling with dplyr and tidyr
text:
Reshaping with tidyr
Analytical tables often alternate between wide and long forms.

pivot_longer()
Use pivot_longer() when multiple columns represent values of the same variable.
library(tidyr)

wide <- tibble(
  model = c("Mazda RX4", "Honda Civic"),
  mpg_2025 = c(21, 30),
  mpg_2026 = c(22, 31)
)

wide |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = starts_with("mpg_"),
    names_to = "year",
    names_prefix = "mpg_",
    values_to = "mpg"
  )
Long form is usually easier for ggplot2, grouped summaries, and time-series operations.


pivot_wider()
Use pivot_wider() when values in a column should become separate fields.
long <- tibble(
  model = c("Mazda RX4", "Mazda RX4", "Honda Civic", "Honda Civic"),
  year = c("2025", "2026", "2025", "2026"),
  mpg = c(21, 22, 30, 31)
)

long |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = year, values_from = mpg)
If more than one value exists for a model-year combination, pivot_wider() will warn or create list-columns. That is a signal to investigate the grain, not a reason to suppress the warning.

title: Schedule and Milestones
text: This course is organized as a sequence of technical and analytical habits. Each module introduces a small set of R ideas, applies them to a business question, and ends with an artifact that can be reviewed by another analyst. The order matters: students learn enough R to inspect an AI draft before they are asked to delegate larger pieces of work.

title: Schedule and Milestones
text:
Course rhythm
Each module follows the same weekly loop:

Read and annotate. Read the assigned chapter and mark the assumptions you expect the code to make.
Run and observe. Execute the examples in the live lab. Record the data shape, output type, and any warnings.
Delegate selectively. Ask an AI assistant for a bounded draft with a stated schema and acceptance tests.
Review and revise. Check the draft against the business question, edge cases, and a small hand-calculated example.
Translate. End with a three-sentence executive takeaway: what changed, what it means, and what decision should follow.

title: Schedule and Milestones
text:
Six-module progression









Module
Focus window
Primary deliverable
Mastery check




1. R Core
Weeks 1–2
A commented script that creates and inspects business vectors, data frames, and functions
Explain every object, type, and subset operation without running an AI rewrite


2. Wrangling
Weeks 3–4
A reproducible tidyverse pipeline with a data contract and join audit
Demonstrate row counts before and after joins and explain the grouping level of every summary


3. Visual Analytics and EDA
Weeks 5–6
An exploratory notebook with a chart sequence and a missing/outlier audit
Justify the chart geometry, transformations, scales, and audience-facing annotation


4. AI Partnership
Weeks 7–8
A prompt log showing schema-first delegation, Socratic tutoring, and debugging iterations
Distinguish a syntactic fix from a business-logic fix and cite the evidence for acceptance


5. Guided Projects
Weeks 9–11
One completed project specification with code, checks, visuals, and executive memo
Meet the project rubric without unexplained warnings, hidden filters, or unsupported claims


6. Capstone Review
Week 12
A polished analytical brief and a reviewer checklist for the next analyst
Reproduce the result, defend the assumptions, and translate the output for a nontechnical stakeholder

title: Schedule and Milestones
text:
Milestone calendar









Milestone
Due point
Evidence to submit
Why it matters




M0: Environment check
Before Module 1
A working R/Quarto setup and one successful Shinylive run
Removes tooling uncertainty before analytical work begins


M1: Schema card
End of Module 1
A table of field names, types, units, and allowed missingness
Makes the data contract visible to both humans and AI tools


M2: Transformation trace
End of Module 2
Before/after row counts and a plain-English pipeline trace
Exposes accidental row multiplication and silent filtering


M3: Visual story
End of Module 3
Two exploratory charts plus a chart-selection rationale
Separates visual decoration from communication design


M4: AI review log
End of Module 4
Prompts, returned code, errors, fixes, and acceptance tests
Assesses process quality rather than whether an AI happened to guess correctly


M5: Project checkpoint
End of Module 5
Completed Milestones 1–3 of a guided project
Creates an early opportunity to catch wrong metrics


M6: Executive memo
End of Module 6
Three-sentence takeaway plus limitations and next action
Connects technical evidence to a responsible business decision

title: Schedule and Milestones
text:
Recommended pacing
The schedule is intentionally compatible with a 12-week term, but the labs can be completed asynchronously. A student who needs more practice should repeat a lab with a new prompt and a new acceptance test rather than skipping ahead. A student who moves quickly should extend the data dictionary, add a sensitivity analysis, or ask the AI tutor to critique the result without rewriting it.

title: Schedule and Milestones
text:
What counts as complete?
A milestone is complete when another person can reproduce the result and understand the reasoning. “The code ran” is necessary but insufficient. Your submission should identify the input rows, transformation decisions, output grain, checks performed, and business interpretation. When an AI assistant contributed code, retain the prompt and explain which parts you accepted, changed, or rejected.

title: Bibliography and External Readings
text: This page records the sources that informed the course architecture, explanations, examples, and tooling. The business scenarios and synthetic datasets in this site are original teaching materials; the links below provide the conceptual and technical foundations we used while building them.

title: Bibliography and External Readings
text:
R and tidyverse foundations

R for Data Science, 2e — Hadley Wickham, Mine Çetinkaya-Rundel, and Garrett Grolemund. The primary curriculum model for workflow, transformation, visualization, exploration, and communication.
R Language Definition — The official reference for R’s evaluation model, objects, environments, functions, and control structures.
R Documentation — A searchable index used to check package functions and example signatures.
dplyr reference — Official documentation for filtering, selecting, mutating, grouping, summarizing, arranging, and joining data.
tidyr reference — Official documentation for tidy data and pivot_longer()/pivot_wider() reshaping.
ggplot2 reference — Official documentation for the Grammar of Graphics, layers, scales, themes, and statistical transformations.
scales reference — Documentation for readable currency, percentage, date, and number formatting.

title: Bibliography and External Readings
text:
Interactive publishing and reproducibility

Quarto documentation — Project configuration, websites, executable documents, publishing, and cross-format authoring.
Shinylive for R — Client-side WebAssembly execution for Shiny applications without a backend R server.
Shinylive Quarto extension — The extension and filter used for the live {shinylive-r} blocks in this site.
GitHub Pages documentation — Hosting and deployment context for the published course site.

title: Bibliography and External Readings

AI-assisted programming and responsible use

OpenAI Codex documentation — Product and workflow documentation consulted for repository-aware AI coding tasks.
GitHub Copilot documentation — Reference for editor-based AI assistance, suggestions, and responsible use.
Anthropic Claude documentation — Reference for conversational coding and context-window practices.
NIST AI Risk Management Framework — A governance reference that informed the course emphasis on validity, transparency, privacy, and accountability.
NIST Generative AI Profile — A companion reference for risks specific to generative systems, including confabulation and human oversight.

title: Bibliography and External Readings
text:
Design references

EECS 280 course materials — The course architecture was inspired by the public-facing structure of a rigorous programming course: clear prerequisites, milestones, project specifications, grading expectations, and reproducibility standards. This site does not reproduce EECS 280 assignments or proprietary materials.
Tidy Data — Hadley Wickham’s paper describing the principles behind tidy data and why consistent structure makes analysis easier to compose.

title: Bibliography and External Readings
text:
How to cite this site
For a course project, cite the page and the underlying source that informed the method. For example: “The pipeline follows the tidy data and transformation conventions described in R4DS, with the business scenario and synthetic data supplied by Intro to R for Business Analytics.” Include the date accessed for web documentation when your institution requires it.

title: Project 1: Regional Sales and Attainment Analysis
text:
You are an analyst supporting a sales operations director. The director believes the organization is “close to target” overall but suspects that a national average is hiding meaningful regional differences. The request is to produce a regional attainment view for the first half of 2026 and identify where a management conversation is warranted.
The central question is: Which regions are above or below target, and what should the director investigate next? Do not claim that the analysis explains the cause of performance. It describes attainment and creates a prioritized question list.

text:
Data dictionary
The source table has one row per region-month.









Field
Type
Definition
Review note




region
character
Commercial region
Expected to be unique within a month


month
character
Calendar month label
Use an explicit ordering, not alphabetical order


sales_usd
numeric
Completed-order net sales in US dollars
Excludes cancelled orders


target_usd
numeric
Monthly sales target in US dollars

title: Project 1: Regional Sales and Attainment Analysis
text:
Technical milestones

Milestone 1: Data cleaning and sanity checks

Confirm one row per region-month.
Parse month as an ordered date or factor.
Check for missing or non-positive targets.
Compare the number of observed region-months with the expected calendar.
Write a short data-quality note before calculating attainment.



Milestone 2: Core aggregation and metric calculation
Calculate regional first-half totals and define attainment as:
[ = ]
Do not average monthly attainment rates unless you can defend equal weighting. Report total sales, total target, attainment, orders, and sales per representative.


Milestone 3: Exploratory visual chart
Create an ordered horizontal bar chart of attainment with a 100% reference line. Add a subtitle stating the period, population, and denominator. Consider a second chart of monthly attainment to distinguish persistent performance from a single-month result.


Milestone 4: Executive memo
Write the three-sentence takeaway required by the course. Include the strongest finding, the business meaning, the next diagnostic question, and one limitation about causality or data coverage.

title: Project 1: Regional Sales and Attainment Analysis
text:
AI prompts in action

Prompt A: schema-first cleaning draft
Write a dplyr pipeline for a table named sales_monthly with one row per
region-month. Fields are region (character), month (character), sales_usd
(numeric), target_usd (numeric), orders (integer), and sales_rep_count (integer).
Return a data-quality audit before the metric calculation. Do not invent dates,
do not drop rows silently, and include checks for duplicate region-month keys,
missing values, and target_usd <= 0. Show the expected output grain.
Expected output: an audit table plus an aggregation pipeline. Verify that the AI did not turn an invalid target into zero or use mean(sales_usd / target_usd) as the primary attainment definition.


Prompt B: metric review
Review this regional attainment calculation as a skeptical finance analyst.
The intended metric is sum(sales_usd) / sum(target_usd), one row per region.
Identify any denominator, grouping, date-window, or NA risk. Return tests and
questions before suggesting a revised line of code.
Expected output: a review checklist, not an unsupported performance narrative. Common pitfalls include averaging ratios, mixing fiscal and calendar periods, and treating missing sales as zero.


Prompt C: visual translation
Given a verified table with region, total_sales, total_target, and attainment,
propose an executive ggplot2 bar chart. Order regions by attainment, format the
y-axis as percentages, add a 100% reference line, and label the period. Explain
how each design choice supports comparison. Do not infer why any region missed target.

Project 2: Customer Retention and Churn Economics
text:
You are an analyst at a subscription business. The retention team knows how many customers churned last month but does not know whether the highest churn rate is also the largest economic risk. Leadership wants a segment-level view that connects customer behavior to recurring revenue and identifies where a retention experiment could have the greatest value.
The central question is: Which customer segment combines meaningful churn exposure with meaningful recurring-revenue risk? The analysis is descriptive. It does not prove that a customer characteristic causes churn.

title: Project 2: Customer Retention and Churn Economics
text:
Technical milestones

Milestone 1: Data cleaning and sanity checks

Confirm customer_id is unique in customers and repeated appropriately in activity.
Check that every activity customer exists in the customer table.
Confirm monthly_fee is non-negative and churned is logical.
State whether churn is measured at the customer level and whether the denominator includes all customers or only customers with observed activity.



Milestone 2: Core aggregation and metric calculation
Join activity to customer attributes, then produce one row per segment with customer count, churned customers, churn rate, recurring revenue, and recurring revenue at risk. Define revenue at risk as the sum of monthly_fee for churned customers; do not multiply churn rate by total revenue unless the weighting is equivalent.


Milestone 3: Exploratory visual chart
Create a quadrant or paired view of churn rate and revenue at risk. Add sample sizes so a high rate based on five customers is not visually treated like a high rate based on five thousand.


Milestone 4: Executive memo
Describe the segment that deserves attention, the evidence supporting that prioritization, the limitation of the observation window, and one retention action that should be tested rather than assumed to work.

title: Project 2: Customer Retention and Churn Economics
text:
AI prompts in action
I have customers (one row per customer) and activity (one row per customer-month).
Customers has customer_id, segment, monthly_fee, tenure_months, acquisition_channel,
and churned. Activity has customer_id, month, sessions, support_tickets, and
last_active_days. Write a dplyr pipeline that verifies key uniqueness, left-joins
activity to customers, and returns one row per segment. Include customer count,
churned count, churn rate, total monthly fee, and monthly fee at risk.
Do not average ratios without explaining the weighting. Return row-count checks and
the expected grain before any code rewrite.
Common pitfalls to verify: joining customer attributes to multiple activity rows and then summing monthly_fee repeatedly; using activity rows rather than customers as the churn denominator; and labeling an association as a retention cause.
For a visual prompt, ask:
Using the verified segment summary, design a two-panel ggplot2 view: churn rate
by segment and monthly recurring revenue at risk by segment. Show customer counts,
use percentages only for the rate panel, and write a subtitle that defines the
observation window. Do not rank segments by churn rate alone.

title: Project 2: Customer Retention and Churn Economics
text:
Interactive project lab
This sandbox includes two linked tables. Try changing a fee or churn flag, then explain why the segment summary changes. A useful extension is to add a minimum customer-count warning.
#| '!! shinylive warning !!': |
#|   shinylive does not work in self-contained HTML documents.
#|   Please set `embed-resources: false` in your metadata.
#| standalone: true
#| components: [editor, viewer]

library(shiny)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)

customers <- data.frame(
  customer_id = paste0("C", 101:112),
  segment = c("Starter", "Starter", "Starter", "Starter", "Growth", "Growth", "Growth", "Growth", "Enterprise", "Enterprise", "Enterprise", "Enterprise"),
  monthly_fee = c(35, 40, 45, 50, 120, 135, 150, 160, 450, 500, 550, 600),
  tenure_months = c(4, 8, 14, 22, 6, 12, 18, 30, 10, 20, 36, 48),
  acquisition_channel = c("Paid", "Organic", "Paid", "Partner", "Organic", "Paid", "Partner", "Organic", "Partner", "Organic", "Paid", "Partner"),
  churned = c(TRUE, FALSE, TRUE, FALSE, FALSE, TRUE, FALSE, FALSE, FALSE, FALSE, TRUE, FALSE)
)

activity <- data.frame(
  customer_id = rep(customers$customer_id, each = 2),
  month = rep(c("May", "June"), times = nrow(customers)),
  sessions = c(2, 1, 8, 7, 4, 2, 12, 10, 18, 16, 20, 21, 6, 5, 14, 13, 40, 42, 35, 38, 24, 8, 30, 29),
  support_tickets = c(1, 2, 0, 1, 2, 1, 0, 0, 3, 2, 1, 1, 0, 0, 2, 2, 1, 0, 0, 1, 2, 4, 0, 0),
  last_active_days = c(20, 28, 4, 6, 12, 20, 3, 4, 8, 6, 5, 4, 18, 25, 7, 8, 2, 3, 4, 4, 6, 30, 3, 4)
)

ui <- fluidPage(
  titlePanel("Churn economics project lab"),
  sidebarLayout(
    sidebarPanel(
      selectInput("segment", "Segment", choices = c("All", unique(customers$segment))),
      helpText("Revenue at risk is the fee of churned customers, counted once per customer.")
    ),
    mainPanel(tableOutput("summary"), plotOutput("plot", height = "430px"))
  )
)

server <- function(input, output, session) {
  output$summary <- renderTable({
    data <- customers
    if (input$segment != "All") data <- data |> filter(segment == input$segment)
    data |>
      group_by(segment) |>
      summarize(
        customers = n(),
        churned = sum(churned),
        churn_rate = mean(churned),
        recurring_revenue = sum(monthly_fee),
        revenue_at_risk = sum(monthly_fee[churned]),
        .groups = "drop"
      )
  })

  output$plot <- renderPlot({
    customers |>
      group_by(segment) |>
      summarize(churn_rate = mean(churned), revenue_at_risk = sum(monthly_fee[churned]), .groups = "drop") |>
      ggplot(aes(churn_rate, revenue_at_risk, label = segment)) +
      geom_point(size = 4, color = "#B54708") +
      geom_text(nudge_y = 25, size = 3) +
      scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::percent_format(accuracy = 1)) +
      labs(x = "Churn rate", y = "Monthly revenue at risk", title = "Prioritize by rate and economic exposure") +
      theme_minimal(base_size = 12)
  })
}

shinyApp(ui, server)

title: Exploratory Data Analysis Workflows
text: Exploratory data analysis (EDA) is a disciplined search for what the data can and cannot support. It is not a hunt for a flattering chart. The output of EDA is a map of distributions, missingness, unusual observations, and relationships that deserve either explanation or a formal test.

title: Exploratory Data Analysis Workflows
text:
The standard EDA pipeline

1. Establish the data contract
Write down the row grain, population, time window, keys, units, and expected ranges. Run glimpse(), summary(), and a duplicate-key check before plotting.
library(dplyr)

glimpse(transactions)
transactions |>
  summarize(
    rows = n(),
    customers = n_distinct(customer_id),
    first_date = min(order_date, na.rm = TRUE),
    last_date = max(order_date, na.rm = TRUE)
  )


2. Check distributions
For numeric fields, inspect center, spread, range, and shape. A mean alone can hide a long tail or a small number of extreme values.
transactions |>
  summarize(
    average_order = mean(order_value, na.rm = TRUE),
    median_order = median(order_value, na.rm = TRUE),
    p90_order = quantile(order_value, 0.90, na.rm = TRUE),
    minimum = min(order_value, na.rm = TRUE),
    maximum = max(order_value, na.rm = TRUE)
  )
Use a histogram or density plot to see the shape. When a variable is strongly skewed, consider whether a median, percentile, log scale, or segmented view better represents the decision.


3. Audit missing values
Missingness is a property of the data-generating process. Create a field-level audit and compare missingness across relevant groups.
missing_audit <- transactions |>
  summarize(across(everything(), ~ sum(is.na(.x)))) |>
  tidyr::pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "field", values_to = "missing_rows") |>
  mutate(missing_rate = missing_rows / nrow(transactions))
Ask whether values are missing completely at random, only for certain channels, or because a process changed. Do not replace missing values with zero without an explicit business definition.


4. Identify outliers
An outlier is an observation that is unusual relative to a chosen reference, not automatically an error. Use multiple views and investigate the source record.
limits <- quantile(transactions$order_value, c(0.25, 0.75), na.rm = TRUE)
iqr_value <- limits[[2]] - limits[[1]]

transactions |>
  filter(
    order_value < limits[[1]] - 1.5 * iqr_value |
      order_value > limits[[2]] + 1.5 * iqr_value
  )
Document whether the outlier is a data error, a legitimate high-value event, or a separate business process. Winsorizing or deleting it changes the question and must be disclosed.


5. Screen multi-variable relationships
Compare numeric measures with scatter plots and grouped summaries. Compare a numeric measure across categories with boxplots or distribution summaries. For time, inspect both level and change.
transactions |>
  group_by(channel) |>
  summarize(
    orders = n(),
    median_value = median(order_value, na.rm = TRUE),
    cancellation_rate = mean(cancelled, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  )
Treat relationships as hypotheses. A strong association can be caused by seasonality, selection, a common driver, or a data-collection rule.

title: Exploratory Data Analysis Workflows
section: EDA as a series of falsification tests
text:
EDA as a series of falsification tests
For each apparent insight, write a competing explanation and a test.








Observation
Competing explanation
Test




Revenue is higher in one region
The region has more customers or a longer observation window
Compare revenue per customer over the same period


Average order value increased
A few unusually large orders shifted the mean
Compare median, percentiles, and trimmed summaries


Churn is higher for one segment
That segment has more missing activity records
Audit missingness and denominator definitions


Delivery time rose in June
June contains more long-distance shipments
Stratify by route, distance, and carrier

title: Exploratory Data Analysis Workflows
text:
AI-assisted EDA without automated storytelling
Ask an AI assistant to propose an EDA plan, not to declare the conclusion. Supply the schema, row grain, data-quality constraints, and decision context. Require it to return: checks, code, expected output shape, and questions that remain unresolved. Then run the checks and write the interpretation yourself.

The Self-Directed Learner: Using AI as a Socratic Tutor
text: An AI assistant becomes a better teacher when you constrain it not to solve the problem immediately. Socratic tutoring keeps the student responsible for the next inference: identify the object, predict the output, choose the grouping level, or explain why a test would fail.

title: The Self-Directed Learner: Using AI as a Socratic Tutor
text:
The tutoring contract
Begin with a role instruction:
Act as a patient R tutor. Do not write the final solution yet.
Ask me one question at a time. Wait for my answer, correct misconceptions
briefly, and use a small synthetic example when needed. Keep the focus on
the business question and the row grain.
Then supply the smallest useful context: the code line, the schema, the error, or the expected output. Do not paste a whole project when one function is enough.

title: The Self-Directed Learner: Using AI as a Socratic Tutor
text:
Prompt templates for productive struggle

Explain a line without replacing it
Explain what line 4 of this pipe does using an analogy from retail inventory.
First identify the input grain and output grain. Do not rewrite the code.
Ask me one question that checks whether I understand the denominator.


Discover grouping logic
Do not write the solution yet. Ask me three guiding questions that help me
write the group_by and summarize logic for one row per region-quarter.
The fields are region, quarter, sales_usd, and target_usd. Include a question
about whether I should average ratios or divide sums.


Predict output before running
Show me a four-row toy table and ask me to predict the result of this mutate
and filter sequence. Do not evaluate it for me until I provide my prediction.
Afterward, compare the prediction with the code's behavior and explain any
difference in terms of vectorized operations and NA values.


Review an explanation
Here is my three-sentence executive summary and the code that produced it.
Act as a skeptical stakeholder. Ask two questions that the summary does not
answer, identify any claim not supported by the code, and suggest one clearer
phrase. Do not change the underlying result.

title: The Self-Directed Learner: Using AI as a Socratic Tutor
text:
A five-turn tutoring protocol

Orient. Ask the assistant to restate the business question and data grain.
Predict. Write your expected output shape and one sample row.
Attempt. Write or edit the smallest code you can.
Compare. Run it and share the output or error, not a vague description.
Generalize. Ask what would change if a field were missing, duplicated, or at a different grain.

If the assistant gives the answer too early, say: “Stop. Replace the solution with one guiding question and wait.” The ability to control the tutoring mode is itself a technical skill.

title: The Self-Directed Learner: Using AI as a Socratic Tutor
text:
Tutor mode versus code-review mode
These modes have different jobs.








Mode
Ask for
Avoid




Tutor
Questions, analogies, predictions, hints, misconceptions
Full rewrites before an attempt


Pair programmer
A bounded draft with assumptions and tests
Vague “make it better” requests


Code reviewer
Risks, edge cases, tests, and unsupported claims
Treating style feedback as correctness evidence


Editor
Labels, structure, and readability improvements
Letting wording change the result



Switch modes explicitly in the prompt. A single conversation can move from tutor to pair programmer, but the handoff should be visible.

title: The Self-Directed Learner: Using AI as a Socratic Tutor
text:
Self-check rubric
Before asking for a solution, can you answer these questions?

What does one row represent right now?
Which field is the denominator, and why?
What should happen to missing, duplicated, or zero-valued records?
What output shape would prove the code worked?
How would you explain the result without naming an R function?

If not, ask the AI to tutor you through those questions. If yes, write the first draft and ask for a review.

title: AI Partnership Framework and Ethics
text:
AI coding assistants are powerful autocomplete systems, reasoning partners, and private tutors. They are not a source of authority about your data or your organization. In this course, an assistant may write a first draft, explain a function, propose a test, or help locate a bug. The student is still responsible for the definition of the metric, the validity of the computation, the protection of the data, and the accuracy of the stakeholder message.
The governing principle is simple:

Delegate keystrokes, not accountability.

title: AI Partnership Framework and Ethics
text:
AI coding assistants are powerful autocomplete systems, reasoning partners, and private tutors. They are not a source of authority about your data or your organization. In this course, an assistant may write a first draft, explain a function, propose a test, or help locate a bug. The student is still responsible for the definition of the metric, the validity of the computation, the protection of the data, and the accuracy of the stakeholder message.
The governing principle is simple:

Delegate keystrokes, not accountability.

title: AI Partnership Framework and Ethics
text:
The AI Code Reviewer Standard
Every AI-assisted submission must pass five gates.

Question gate. State the decision the analysis is meant to support. A prompt that asks for “interesting insights” is not a business specification.
Schema gate. Provide field names, types, units, grain, and permitted missingness. Do not upload confidential raw records merely to avoid describing the schema.
Computation gate. Inspect the generated pipeline line by line. Confirm filters, joins, grouping levels, denominators, date windows, and NA behavior.
Evidence gate. Run small tests that could falsify the result: row counts, duplicate checks, hand calculations, known totals, and edge cases.
Translation gate. Explain the result in plain English, including uncertainty and a next action. A chart or a console table is not an executive conclusion.

An AI-generated script that fails one of these gates is a draft, not an answer.

title: AI Partnership Framework and Ethics
text:
Responsible use policy

Allowed uses

Asking an assistant to explain R syntax, propose a tidyverse pipeline, or compare two chart designs.
Supplying a synthetic dataset or a schema-only description to obtain a reproducible example.
Pasting a complete error message and the smallest relevant code snippet for root-cause analysis.
Asking the assistant to generate tests, assumptions, and questions that you then verify independently.



Uses that require care

Copying organizational data into a tool that has not been approved for that data classification.
Accepting a statistical result because the code is polished or because the assistant sounds confident.
Presenting an AI-generated causal explanation when the analysis only shows association.
Using a generated chart without checking its denominator, time period, population, or excluded rows.



Not acceptable

Treating an AI response as a citation or as evidence that a number is correct.
Hiding AI assistance when a course, employer, or client requires disclosure.
Uploading personally identifiable, proprietary, regulated, or credential information into an unapproved service.
Submitting code that the analyst cannot explain or reproduce.

title: AI Partnership Framework and Ethics
text:
Hallucination patterns in business statistics
AI systems often produce code that is syntactically valid and economically wrong. Watch for these patterns:








Risk
What the code may do
Verification question




Silent NA removal
mean(x, na.rm = TRUE) calculates a value on an unknown subset
How many observations were removed, and could missingness be systematic?


Mean of ratios
Averages store-level conversion rates with equal weight
Should the result be a ratio of totals, weighted by opportunities or transactions?


Wrong join grain
Joins a customer table to a transaction table and repeats customer attributes
What is the expected row count and key uniqueness before and after the join?


Hidden grouping
Leaves a prior group_by() active while calculating a supposedly global metric
What is the grouping structure immediately before summarize()?


Date ambiguity
Treats a fiscal quarter or local timestamp as a calendar date
Which timezone, fiscal calendar, and boundary convention apply?


Directional claim
Describes correlation as a driver or cause
What design or evidence supports causality?



The correction is not “ask the AI to be more accurate.” The correction is to specify the denominator, grain, missingness rule, and acceptance test.

title: AI Partnership Framework and Ethics
section: Schema-first prompting without raw data leakage
text:
Schema-first prompting without raw data leakage
Before asking for code, create a compact schema card. It can be generated locally with glimpse() and str() and then edited to remove sensitive values.
glimpse(transactions)
str(transactions)

transactions |>
  summarise(
    rows = n(),
    across(everything(), ~ sum(is.na(.x)))
  )
Share information such as customer_id: character, one row per transaction, not for modeling, not the actual customer IDs. Include units (revenue_usd), allowed values (channel is one of store, web, partner), and key relationships (customer_id repeats in transactions; product_id is unique in products). A useful schema prompt also states the expected output grain and the business decision.

title: AI Partnership Framework and Ethics
text:
Plain-English translation requirement
Every meaningful result ends with exactly three sentences:

Finding: what changed or differs, with the population and time window.
Meaning: why that pattern matters to the stakeholder, including the metric definition.
Action: what to investigate or do next, plus the most important limitation.

For example: “West-region revenue grew 12% from Q1 to Q2 across 184 completed orders. Growth came primarily from higher order volume, while average order value was broadly stable. Prioritize a review of West-region fulfillment capacity before expanding promotion spend, because cancelled orders were excluded from the current calculation.”

title: AI Partnership Framework and Ethics
text:
Grading and mastery








Criterion
Weight
Full-credit evidence




Code accuracy and reproducibility
40%
The script runs from a clean session, preserves the stated grain, handles edge cases, and includes checks


Visual clarity and honesty
25%
The graphic uses an appropriate geometry, readable scales, useful labels, and no misleading transformations


Executive summary quality
25%
The three-sentence summary states a supported finding, business meaning, action, and limitation


AI process documentation
10%
Prompts, revisions, rejected suggestions, and verification steps are recorded

title: AI Partnership Framework and Ethics
text:
A review conversation
When reviewing a classmate’s AI-assisted work, ask: “What would have to be true for this number to be correct?” Then inspect the code for those conditions. Good review is specific, respectful, and evidence-based: point to a field, a line, a row count, or a chart scale. The aim is not to punish the use of AI; it is to make the analyst’s reasoning visible.

title: Verification, Debugging, and Sanity Checking
text: Debugging is the process of narrowing the difference between the intended analysis and the observed behavior. An AI assistant can shorten the search, but it cannot decide whether the intended behavior was correct. Your job is to preserve the evidence and ask for a root-cause analysis.

title: Verification, Debugging, and Sanity Checking
text:
The complete debugging loop

Run the smallest reproducible example. Reduce the data and code until the failure remains.
Copy the complete error. Include the error class, message, and the line or call named in the traceback.
Add context. Share the relevant code, object classes, dimensions, and expected behavior. Remove sensitive values.
Ask for causes before fixes. Require two or three plausible causes, a test for each, and the smallest change.
Apply one change. Do not accept a wholesale rewrite that makes it impossible to know what fixed the issue.
Run acceptance tests. Confirm the original error is gone and the business meaning is unchanged.
Record the lesson. Add the cause, fix, and prevention check to the prompt log.

title: Verification, Debugging, and Sanity Checking
text:
Syntax errors versus logic errors
A syntax error prevents R from parsing or evaluating an expression. A logic error produces a result that looks reasonable but answers the wrong question.








Signal
Likely category
Example check




unexpected ')'
Syntax
Balance parentheses and commas


object 'x' not found
Scope or naming
Inspect object creation and spelling


could not find function
Package or namespace
Load the package or use pkg::fn()


Output has too many rows after a join
Logic/grain
Check key uniqueness and row counts


Result changes dramatically after na.rm = TRUE
Data/method
Report missing count and compare denominators


Plot is correct but misleadingly labeled
Communication
Compare title, scale, population, and metric

title: Verification, Debugging, and Sanity Checking
Verification, Debugging, and Sanity Checking
section: Sanity checks that belong in production code

title: Verification, Debugging, and Sanity Checking
section: Read the console like an investigator
text:
Read the console like an investigator
Warnings are evidence. A warning about an unmatched join, a coercion, or removed rows can change the result without stopping execution. Copy the warning into the review log and decide whether it is expected. A clean console is not proof of a correct analysis; a noisy console is a request for an explanation.

title: Verification, Debugging, and Sanity Checking
text:
Final review questions

Can another analyst reproduce the error from the shared snippet?
Did the fix address the root cause or merely suppress the message?
Did row count, grain, denominators, and missingness behavior change?
Does the corrected result pass a hand calculation on a tiny example?
Did the stakeholder summary change after the fix?

title: Setting Up and Prompting Modern AI Agents
text: An AI coding agent is most useful when it has enough context to be precise and not enough access to create avoidable risk. This chapter describes a tool-agnostic setup for ChatGPT/Codex, Claude, or GitHub Copilot. Product names and interface labels change; the durable ideas are account hygiene, scoped context, reproducible prompts, and reviewable outputs.
crumbs: Setting Up and Prompting Modern AI Agents

title: Setting Up and Prompting Modern AI Agents
text:
1. Choose an approved assistant
Use the assistant permitted by your course or organization. Common options include:

ChatGPT and Codex for conversational analysis, code review, and repository-aware tasks.
Claude for long-form explanation and code discussion.
GitHub Copilot for in-editor completion and chat.

Read the current product documentation before installation. Do not install an extension or desktop application from an unverified mirror, and do not paste credentials, access tokens, or proprietary datasets into a tool whose data policy you have not checked.
crumbs: Setting Up and Prompting Modern AI Agents

title: Setting Up and Prompting Modern AI Agents
text:
2. Account and privacy setup

Create or sign into the account using the identity approved for coursework.
Review data controls, retention settings, and workspace sharing before uploading any content.
Turn on multi-factor authentication where available.
Use a synthetic dataset or a schema card for practice. Replace customer IDs, emails, addresses, and transaction-level values with placeholders.
Record which model or assistant produced a material code draft when your organization requires provenance.

The goal is not to eliminate AI use. It is to make the boundary between the assistant and the organization’s data explicit.
crumbs: Setting Up and Prompting Modern AI Agents

title: Setting Up and Prompting Modern AI Agents
crumbs: Setting Up and Prompting Modern AI Agents

title: Setting Up and Prompting Modern AI Agents
section: 4. The first prompt should establish a contract
text:
4. The first prompt should establish a contract
Use a prompt that gives the assistant a role, a question, a schema, constraints, and an output contract.
You are a careful R business analyst and code reviewer.

Business question: Which region improved sales attainment from Q1 to Q2?
Data grain: one row per region-quarter.
Fields: region (character), quarter (character), sales_usd (numeric), target_usd (numeric).
Packages allowed: dplyr, tidyr, ggplot2, scales.
Constraints: do not invent fields; handle zero targets explicitly; retain a row-count check.
Return: (1) R code, (2) expected output grain, (3) three verification tests, and (4) one limitation.
Do not claim causality.
If the tool returns code without the requested tests or output grain, the prompt was not fulfilled. Ask for a revision rather than silently filling the gaps yourself.
crumbs: Setting Up and Prompting Modern AI Agents

title: Setting Up and Prompting Modern AI Agents
section: 5. Capture the conversation as analysis evidence
text:
5. Capture the conversation as analysis evidence
Keep a small prompt log with the date, purpose, input schema, assistant output, revisions, errors, and acceptance decision. The log is not busywork. It lets you reconstruct why a line exists and helps a future analyst distinguish an intentional assumption from an AI default.







Log field
Example




Business question
Compare quarterly attainment by region


Context supplied
Schema card and row grain; no raw customer data


AI request
Generate a dplyr pipeline plus tests


Review finding
AI used mean of regional ratios; changed to ratio of totals


Evidence
Hand calculation for two regions and join-count check


Decision
Accepted revised pipeline with explicit denominator
crumbs: Setting Up and Prompting Modern AI Agents

title: Setting Up and Prompting Modern AI Agents
text:
6. A disciplined prompt loop
Use this sequence for almost any R task:

Specify. Describe the decision, schema, grain, packages, and output.
Draft. Ask for the smallest runnable code that answers one sub-question.
Explain. Ask the assistant to annotate assumptions and expected output shape.
Run. Execute the code in RStudio, Quarto, or the Shinylive sandbox.
Test. Compare counts, totals, and edge cases to independent expectations.
Refine. Return only the error or failing test with the relevant snippet.
Translate. Write the stakeholder summary yourself, then ask the assistant to critique clarity without changing the claim.

The assistant is a collaborator in the loop, not the owner of the loop.
crumbs: Setting Up and Prompting Modern AI Agents

title: Automated Visual Refinement: Prompting for Executive Visuals
text: An AI assistant can make a ggplot2 draft more readable, but “prettier” is not a specification. Visual refinement should preserve the analytical meaning while improving hierarchy, labeling, scale interpretation, and audience fit.

title: Automated Visual Refinement: Prompting for Executive Visuals
text:
Start with a chart brief
Before prompting, write a brief:
Audience: regional sales director
Decision: choose where to investigate missed target attainment
Population: completed orders, January–June 2026
Grain: one row per region-month before aggregation
Metric: attainment = sum(sales_usd) / sum(target_usd)
Chart: ordered horizontal bars, one bar per region
Must show: percent scale, target reference at 100%, data period, source note
Must not imply: that attainment explains why performance changed
This prevents the assistant from deciding that a pie chart, a 3-D effect, or a dramatic color scale is an appropriate answer.

title: Automated Visual Refinement: Prompting for Executive Visuals
text:
Iterative styling sequence
Ask for one controlled change per turn and run the result after each change.

1. Format currency and percentages
Keep the data and geometry unchanged. Format revenue with scales::dollar_format()
and attainment with scales::percent_format(accuracy = 1%). Explain which field
is being formatted and confirm that formatting does not change the underlying values.


2. Re-order factor bars
Re-order the region factor by attainment so the lowest region appears first in
a horizontal bar chart. Use reorder() or forcats::fct_reorder(), retain the
original region labels, and explain whether the ordering is based on weighted
attainment or an average of region-level ratios.


3. Add context without adding claims
Add a subtitle stating the period, population, and metric denominator. Add a
caption for the data source and a note that attainment is descriptive. Do not
change the title into a causal or predictive claim.


4. Apply professional styling
Use a minimal theme, one accent color for the focal comparison, a neutral color
for context, readable text, and a target reference line at 100%. Remove minor
grid lines only if the values remain easy to compare. Return the code and list
each visual decision in plain English.

title: Automated Visual Refinement: Prompting for Executive Visuals
text:
Review the revised chart
Use this checklist after every AI-generated revision:

Is the population and period unchanged?
Does the axis label include the unit and denominator?
Does the scale preserve meaningful differences?
Are categories ordered by the stated metric, not alphabetically by accident?
Does color encode a meaningful variable, or merely attract attention?
Is the reference line defined and on the same scale as the bars?
Does the title describe the evidence without implying causality?
Can a reader identify the source, exclusions, and missing-data rule?

title: Automated Visual Refinement: Prompting for Executive Visuals
text:
Prompting for an executive summary
Do not ask: “What does this chart say?” Ask:
Here is the verified summary table and the final ggplot code. Draft two candidate
three-sentence executive takeaways. Sentence 1 must state the comparison and
period. Sentence 2 must describe the business implication without causal language.
Sentence 3 must name one limitation or next check. Do not introduce any number
not present in the table. Label each candidate so I can select and edit it.
The analyst must still select the wording. A well-written sentence can be wrong if the chart uses the wrong denominator.

title: Automated Visual Refinement: Prompting for Executive Visuals
section: Live lab: one change at a time
text:
Live lab: one change at a time
The application begins with a basic chart. Use the controls to apply the kinds of revisions you might request from an AI assistant, then describe which change improved communication and which assumption still needs verification.
#| '!! shinylive warning !!': |
#|   shinylive does not work in self-contained HTML documents.
#|   Please set `embed-resources: false` in your metadata.
#| standalone: true
#| components: [editor, viewer]

library(shiny)
library(ggplot2)

attainment <- data.frame(
  region = c("North", "South", "East", "West"),
  sales = c(420000, 385000, 455000, 310000),
  target = c(400000, 400000, 430000, 350000)
)

attainment$rate <- attainment$sales / attainment$target

ui <- fluidPage(
  titlePanel("Executive visual refinement"),
  sidebarLayout(
    sidebarPanel(
      checkboxInput("polished", "Apply polished styling", value = FALSE),
      checkboxInput("ordered", "Order bars by attainment", value = FALSE),
      helpText("Treat each checkbox as a separate prompt and inspect the result.")
    ),
    mainPanel(plotOutput("plot", height = "450px"))
  )
)

server <- function(input, output, session) {
  output$plot <- renderPlot({
    data <- attainment
    if (isTRUE(input$ordered)) data$region <- reorder(data$region, data$rate)

    p <- ggplot(data, aes(x = region, y = rate)) +
      geom_col(fill = "#176B87")

    if (isTRUE(input$polished)) {
      p <- p +
        geom_hline(yintercept = 1, linetype = "dashed", color = "#555555") +
        scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent_format(accuracy = 1)) +
        labs(
          title = "West is furthest below sales target",
          subtitle = "Attainment equals sales divided by target; January-June 2026",
          x = NULL,
          y = "Target attainment",
          caption = "Dashed line indicates 100% attainment"
        ) +
        theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
        theme(panel.grid.minor = element_blank())
    } else {
      p <- p + labs(x = "Region", y = "rate")
    }
    p
  })
}

shinyApp(ui, server)

title: Intro to R for Business Analytics
Intro to R for Business Analytics
Intro to R for Business Analytics
text:
Teaching philosophy
The course uses a Code Reviewer framework. Every script is treated as a proposal that must be inspected. The analyst is accountable for correctness even when an AI writes the first draft. We value reproducible evidence over clever syntax, explicit assumptions over confident prose, and useful questions over premature conclusions.
The learning loop is:
Business question → data contract → small code draft → run and inspect
→ verify grain, counts, denominators, and edge cases → visualize
→ translate for a stakeholder → record the decision and limitation

title: Intro to R for Business Analytics
text:
The AI Code Reviewer Standard
AI assistance is permitted and expected when used transparently. It cannot replace the following responsibilities:

Define the population, time window, metric, and decision.
Protect sensitive data by sharing schemas or synthetic examples instead of raw records.
Check joins, grouping levels, missing values, zero denominators, duplicate keys, and date boundaries.
Test generated code on a tiny hand-calculated example.
Explain what the output means and what it does not establish.

Students should keep a prompt log for substantial work: the request, schema supplied, returned code, errors, changes, and acceptance tests. If the assistant’s suggestion is rejected, record why. Rejection is evidence of analytical judgment.

Grading and mastery metrics








Category
Weight
What mastery looks like




Code accuracy and reproducibility
40%

title: Intro to R for Business Analytics
text:
Plain-English translation requirement
Every project must end with three sentences:

Finding: what happened, for which population, and during which period.
Meaning: why the pattern matters, using the defined metric.
Action: what to investigate or do next, plus the most important limitation.

Avoid function names, unexplained acronyms, causal verbs, and numbers that do not appear in the verified output.

title: Intro to R for Business Analytics
text:
How to use this site
Start with Schedule and Milestones, then work through the R Foundations in order. The AI mastery pages provide reusable prompts and review patterns. The guided projects are specifications, not answer keys: use the sandbox to test your own draft, and keep your evidence with the final memo.

title: Project 3: Supply Chain Logistics and Bottlenecks
text:
You are supporting a distribution network that has missed delivery promises in several lanes. The operations director needs to know whether the bottleneck is concentrated in a carrier, a warehouse, or a route. The director also wants to avoid “fixing” the lane with the highest late rate if that lane has very little volume.
The central question is: Where is service risk concentrated when both late-delivery rate and shipment volume are considered? The analysis should prioritize investigation; it should not claim that a carrier or warehouse caused the delay without process evidence.

title: Project 3: Supply Chain Logistics and Bottlenecks

You are supporting a distribution network that has missed delivery promises in several lanes. The operations director needs to know whether the bottleneck is concentrated in a carrier, a warehouse, or a route. The director also wants to avoid “fixing” the lane with the highest late rate if that lane has very little volume.
The central question is: Where is service risk concentrated when both late-delivery rate and shipment volume are considered? The analysis should prioritize investigation; it should not claim that a carrier or warehouse caused the delay without process evidence.

title: Project 3: Supply Chain Logistics and Bottlenecks
text:
Data dictionary
The main table has one row per shipment.



Field
Type
Definition




shipment_id
character
Unique shipment key


warehouse
character
Origin fulfillment center


route
character
Destination lane or route code


carrier
character
Delivery carrier


ship_date
character
Date shipment left the warehouse


promised_days
integer
Service promise in days


actual_days
integer
Observed transit time in days


shipping_cost_usd
numeric
Shipment-level transportation cost


units
integer
Units shipped


priority
character
Standard or expedited service



Derived fields include late = actual_days > promised_days, delay_days = actual_days - promised_days, and cost_per_unit = shipping_cost_usd / units. A negative delay is early delivery, not a missing value.

title: Project 3: Supply Chain Logistics and Bottlenecks
text:
Technical milestones

Milestone 1: Data cleaning and sanity checks

Confirm shipment_id is unique.
Check dates, positive units, non-negative costs, and plausible transit times.
Confirm promised and actual days use the same business-day convention.
Check whether any route-carrier combination has too few shipments for a stable rate.



Milestone 2: Core aggregation and metric calculation
Produce one row per warehouse-route-carrier combination with shipments, late shipments, late rate, average delay among late shipments, total units, and total shipping cost. Distinguish mean(late) from the share of late shipments and show the denominator.


Milestone 3: Exploratory visual chart
Build a volume-versus-late-rate scatter plot with point size representing shipments and labels for the most material lanes. Add a second view of average delay or cost per unit only after defining its population.


Milestone 4: Executive memo
Recommend one operational investigation. Name the evidence, the decision it informs, the data limitation, and the next measurement needed to determine root cause.
crumbs: Project 3: Supply Chain Logistics and Bottlenecks

title: Project 3: Supply Chain Logistics and Bottlenecks
text:
AI prompts in action
I have a shipment table with one row per shipment and these fields: shipment_id,
warehouse, route, carrier, promised_days, actual_days, shipping_cost_usd, units,
and priority. Write a dplyr workflow that audits unique shipment IDs and invalid
units/costs, creates late and delay_days, and summarizes one row per
warehouse-route-carrier. Include shipment count, late count, late rate, mean delay
among late shipments, total units, and cost per unit. State every denominator and
do not infer a root cause.
Ask a second pass:
Review this bottleneck chart specification. I want to prioritize lanes using both
volume and late rate. Identify how a small denominator, a high-volume route, or
an unequal mix of priority shipments could distort the recommendation. Propose
three sensitivity checks; do not rewrite the chart yet.
Common pitfalls include calculating average delay across on-time shipments, ranking by late rate alone, and summing shipping cost after a many-to-many join.

title: R Core: Syntax, Types, and Structures
text: R is a language for describing objects and transformations. In business analytics, the important question is not whether you can memorize every function. It is whether you can look at a script and explain what each object represents, what shape it has, and how a transformation changes the evidence available for a decision.
crumbs: R Core: Syntax, Types, and Structures

title: R Core: Syntax, Types, and Structures
text:
1. Names and assignment
Use <- to assign a value to a name. Read the statement as “store the value on the right under the name on the left.” Names should describe business meaning rather than implementation details.
unit_price <- 42.50
units_sold <- 18
revenue <- unit_price * units_sold
revenue
R is case-sensitive: revenue and Revenue are different names. Avoid names that shadow common functions such as mean, data, or c. Use snake_case consistently, and keep a clear distinction between raw fields (units_sold) and derived metrics (revenue).
crumbs: R Core: Syntax, Types, and Structures

title: R Core: Syntax, Types, and Structures
text:
2. Atomic data types
The most common atomic types are numeric, character, logical, and date-like values. Use typeof() for the underlying storage type and class() for the object’s higher-level behavior.








Type
Example
Business use




Numeric
1250.50, 3L
Revenue, quantity, score, count


Character
"North"
Labels, codes, free text


Logical
TRUE, FALSE
Flags and conditions


Missing
NA
Unknown or unrecorded value


Factor
factor(c("Web", "Store"))
A categorical variable with known levels


Date
as.Date("2026-01-15")
Time windows and ordering



R will often coerce values to a common type when you combine them. c(1, "2") becomes a character vector because a character value cannot be stored as numeric without loss of information. Do not let automatic coercion decide the meaning of a field silently; inspect it.
typeof(42.5)
typeof("42.5")
is.numeric(42.5)
is.character("42.5")
as.numeric("42.5")
crumbs: R Core: Syntax, Types, and Structures

title: R Core: Syntax, Types, and Structures
text:
3. Vectors and indexing
Most R objects begin as vectors: ordered collections of values of one type. The c() function combines values, and square brackets select positions or names.
regions <- c("North", "South", "West")
targets <- c(North = 100000, South = 85000, West = 92000)

regions[1]
targets["West"]
targets[targets > 90000]
length(targets)
Indexing begins at 1. Logical indexing is especially useful for business filters, but remember that NA in a logical condition can produce an NA result rather than TRUE or FALSE.
margin <- c(0.32, NA, 0.18, 0.41)
margin > 0.25
margin[!is.na(margin) & margin > 0.25]
crumbs: R Core: Syntax, Types, and Structures

title: R Core: Syntax, Types, and Structures
text:
4. Data frames and tibbles
A data frame is a rectangular object: each column is a vector, and all columns have the same number of rows. A row is an observation at a particular grain. Before writing a summary, state the grain in plain English: “one row per order,” “one row per customer-month,” or “one row per store-quarter.”
orders <- data.frame(
  order_id = c("A01", "A02", "A03"),
  region = c("North", "North", "West"),
  units = c(2, 5, 1),
  revenue = c(80, 250, 45)
)

nrow(orders)
ncol(orders)
names(orders)
orders$revenue
orders[orders$units >= 2, ]
The tidyverse uses tibbles, which print more safely in a console and preserve useful metadata. tibble::as_tibble(orders) converts a data frame. In a table, orders$revenue extracts a vector; orders["revenue"] extracts a one-column table. This distinction matters when a function expects a vector.
crumbs: R Core: Syntax, Types, and Structures

title: R Core: Syntax, Types, and Structures
text:
5. Missing values and comparisons
NA means “unknown,” not zero, not false, and not “not applicable” unless your data dictionary explicitly says so. Most arithmetic involving NA returns NA. Functions such as sum() and mean() can remove missing values with na.rm = TRUE, but you must report how many values were removed.
scores <- c(0.80, 0.72, NA, 0.91)
mean(scores)
mean(scores, na.rm = TRUE)
sum(is.na(scores))
Use is.na(x) to test for missingness. Do not use x == NA; the result of that comparison is NA, not a usable logical answer.
crumbs: R Core: Syntax, Types, and Structures

title: R Core: Syntax, Types, and Structures
text:
6. Functions and control flow
Functions package a repeatable transformation. Name the inputs and make the return value clear. A function is a useful unit for both human review and AI-assisted testing.
attainment <- function(actual, target) {
  ifelse(target == 0, NA_real_, actual / target)
}

attainment(c(90, 110), c(100, 100))
Use if when you need one branch of code to run and ifelse() or dplyr::if_else() when you need a vectorized result. for loops are valid, but vectorized functions, summarise(), and mutate() usually express business transformations more clearly.
crumbs: R Core: Syntax, Types, and Structures

title: R Core: Syntax, Types, and Structures
text:
7. A repeatable inspection checklist
Before trusting an object, inspect:
class(orders)
str(orders)
head(orders)
summary(orders)
Ask four questions: What is the object’s type? What is its row grain? Which columns can be missing? What should happen if the object is empty? These questions are the foundation for directing an AI assistant.

section: Live lab: read the object before changing it
text:
Live lab: read the object before changing it
Run the application, inspect the structure output, and change the minimum-revenue filter. The exercise is deliberately small: your goal is to predict the result before you click Run.
#| '!! shinylive warning !!': |
#|   shinylive does not work in self-contained HTML documents.
#|   Please set `embed-resources: false` in your metadata.
#| standalone: true
#| components: [editor, viewer]

library(shiny)

orders <- data.frame(
  order_id = c("A01", "A02", "A03", "A04"),
  region = c("North", "North", "West", "West"),
  units = c(2, 5, 1, 4),
  revenue = c(80, 250, 45, 220),
  repeat_customer = c(TRUE, FALSE, TRUE, FALSE)
)

ui <- fluidPage(
  titlePanel("R core inspection lab"),
  sidebarLayout(
    sidebarPanel(
      numericInput("minimum", "Minimum revenue", value = 100, min = 0),
      helpText("Change the threshold, then explain which rows remain.")
    ),
    mainPanel(
      h4("Object structure"),
      verbatimTextOutput("structure"),
      h4("Filtered orders"),
      tableOutput("selected")
    )
  )
)

server <- function(input, output, session) {
  output$structure <- renderPrint({
    str(orders)
  })

  output$selected <- renderTable({
    orders[orders$revenue >= input$minimum, ]
  })
}

shinyApp(ui, server)

title: Open Analytical Sandbox
Visual Analytics with ggplot2
text: ggplot2 implements the Grammar of Graphics. A plot is not a single picture produced by a magic command; it is a set of explicit decisions about data, visual mappings, geometries, statistical transformations, coordinates, facets, and themes. Making those decisions explicit is what lets an analyst review an AI-generated chart.

title: Visual Analytics with ggplot2
text:
The layers of the grammar

1. Data
Start with a rectangular table and state its grain. A chart of transactions and a chart of customer summaries answer different questions even if they use the same columns.
library(ggplot2)

ggplot(data = mtcars)


2. Aesthetics
aes() maps variables to visual properties such as x-position, y-position, color, fill, size, or shape.
ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = wt, y = mpg, color = factor(cyl)))
Mapping a variable inside aes() creates a data-driven legend. Setting a constant outside aes() applies the same value to every observation.


3. Geometries
Geometries choose how observations become marks: geom_point() for individual observations, geom_col() for precomputed bar heights, geom_bar() for counts, and geom_line() for ordered sequences.
ggplot(mtcars, aes(wt, mpg)) +
  geom_point()
Use geom_col() when your data already contains the metric to display. Use geom_bar() when you want ggplot2 to count rows or calculate a statistic.


4. Facets
Facets split a chart into comparable panels. They are useful when a single encoding would create too much visual overlap.
ggplot(mtcars, aes(wt, mpg)) +
  geom_point() +
  facet_wrap(~ factor(cyl))
Facets are not a substitute for a definition of the comparison. Check whether panel scales should be fixed or allowed to vary.


5. Statistical transformations
Some geoms calculate summaries. A histogram bins observations, a boxplot calculates quartiles, and stat_summary() can show a mean or interval. Be explicit when a statistical transformation changes the unit of analysis.
ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = factor(cyl), y = mpg)) +
  stat_summary(fun = mean, geom = "col")
This chart shows mean MPG by cylinder group, not the individual vehicle values. Label it accordingly.


6. Coordinates
Coordinates control the spatial system. coord_flip() is useful for long category labels, while coord_cartesian() zooms without dropping observations from statistical calculations.
ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = factor(cyl), y = mpg)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  coord_flip()
Do not use scale_y_continuous(limits = ...) to zoom a distribution unless you intend to remove observations before the statistic is calculated.


7. Themes and labels
Themes control non-data ink. Labels provide the context the audience needs to interpret the data encoding.
ggplot(mtcars, aes(wt, mpg)) +
  geom_point() +
  labs(
    title = "Fuel efficiency declines as vehicle weight increases",
    subtitle = "Motor Trend car data; each point represents one model",
    x = "Weight (1,000 lb)",
    y = "Miles per gallon",
    color = "Cylinders"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

title: Visual Analytics with ggplot2
section: Before and after: an executive sales chart
text:
Before and after: an executive sales chart
The default chart may be technically correct but still hard to read. The polished version defines a business title, formats currency, removes unnecessary decoration, and uses a meaningful ordering.

Before
ggplot(store_sales, aes(store, revenue)) +
  geom_col()


After
library(dplyr)
library(scales)

store_sales |>
  mutate(store = reorder(store, revenue)) |>
  ggplot(aes(store, revenue)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#176B87", width = 0.7) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = label_dollar(scale = 1e-3, suffix = "K")) +
  labs(
    title = "Downtown leads store revenue",
    subtitle = "Net revenue, January–June 2026; stores ordered low to high",
    x = NULL,
    y = "Revenue (thousands of dollars)",
    caption = "Source: internal transaction extract"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 30, hjust = 1)
  )
The code does not make the business claim by itself. The title is a claim that must be supported by the filtered population, period, currency definition, and aggregation.

title: Visual Analytics with ggplot2
section: Choosing a chart for a question
text:
Choosing a chart for a question








Question
Useful geometry
Review concern




How are two numeric measures related?
Scatter plot with optional trend line
Association is not causation; check overplotting and outliers


How do categories compare?
Ordered bar chart
Use a common baseline and label the unit


How does a measure change over time?
Line chart
Sort dates and state the period definition


How does a distribution differ by group?
Boxplot, violin, or histogram
Show sample size and preserve the scale


Which part contributes to a total?
Stacked bar or dot plot
Avoid hard-to-compare segments when ranking matters

title: Visual Analytics with ggplot2
text:
Live lab: default versus publication-ready
Use the selector to switch between a default scatter plot and a deliberately styled executive version. Ask an AI assistant to suggest one change at a time, then verify whether the change improves the intended comparison.
#| '!! shinylive warning !!': |
#|   shinylive does not work in self-contained HTML documents.
#|   Please set `embed-resources: false` in your metadata.
#| standalone: true
#| components: [editor, viewer]

library(shiny)
library(ggplot2)

sales <- data.frame(
  store = c("Airport", "Downtown", "Lakeside", "Market", "Northside", "Riverside"),
  revenue = c(118000, 184000, 97000, 151000, 132000, 109000),
  margin = c(0.21, 0.24, 0.18, 0.22, 0.20, 0.19),
  transactions = c(3900, 5200, 3100, 4600, 4200, 3500)
)

ui <- fluidPage(
  titlePanel("Visual refinement lab"),
  sidebarLayout(
    sidebarPanel(
      radioButtons("style", "Chart style", choices = c("Default", "Executive"), inline = TRUE),
      helpText("Describe one visual difference and one business implication.")
    ),
    mainPanel(plotOutput("chart", height = "480px"))
  )
)

server <- function(input, output, session) {
  output$chart <- renderPlot({
    p <- ggplot(sales, aes(x = transactions, y = revenue, label = store)) +
      geom_point(size = 3, color = "#176B87")

    if (input$style == "Executive") {
      p <- p +
        geom_text(nudge_y = 5000, size = 3) +
        scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_dollar()) +
        labs(
          title = "Higher transaction volume is associated with higher revenue",
          subtitle = "Six stores; net revenue and completed transactions",
          x = "Completed transactions",
          y = "Net revenue"
        ) +
        theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
        theme(panel.grid.minor = element_blank())
    }

    p
  })
}

shinyApp(ui, server)
